extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students of comedy, comedians and writers interested in anti-humor
extracted.subtask_description: Characteristics and production/identification guidance for anti-humor (anti-comedy): a style of alternative comedy that relies on absence or reversal of expected joke structures to produce an effect. Useful for performers, writers, and analysts of stand-up and narrative jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise factor: absence of expected joke or punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor ... is a type of alternative humor that is based on the surprise factor of absence of an expected joke or of a punch line in a narration that is set up as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core technique is to set up a conventional joke structure (setup suggesting a punchline) and then omit or subvert the expected punchline; this absence itself is the source of the comedic (or other emotional) effect. The page notes this can produce humor for some audiences but is deliberately contrary to standard joke payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticlimax / shaggy dog (the yarn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The yarn, also called a shaggy dog story, is a type of anti-humor that involves telling an extremely long joke with an intricate (and sometimes grisly) back story and surreal or repetitive plotline, before ending the story with either a weak spoonerism, or abruptly stopping with no real punchline at all, or no soap radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long, detailed, often meandering narrative that builds expectation; end with an intentionally weak, trivial, or absent payoff (e.g., a spoonerism or abrupt stop). The anticlimax—an extended setup leading to little or no payoff—is the defining device here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious punchline (meta-obvious payoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obvious punchline involves narratives that are structured like a traditional joke including a set-up and punchline, but whose punchline is the most obvious to the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver a punchline that is literal/banal and therefore anti-climactic (examples: 'Why did the chicken cross the road?' or dialogic 'What did the farmer say when he lost his tractor?' — reply: 'Where's my tractor?'). The humor arises from deflating the expectation of cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provoking non-humorous emotions via reversal of expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor is described as a form of irony or reversal of expectations that may provoke an emotion opposite to humor, such as fear, pain, embarrassment, disgust, awkwardness, or discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators can aim not merely to surprise but to elicit discomfort, embarrassment, or other negative/ambivalent reactions by violating the usual payoff rules of jokes. Be aware audiences vary in whether they find this funny or off-putting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodying the traditional idea of the joke (alternative comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative comedy, among its other aspects, parodies the traditional idea of the joke as a form of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-humor functions as a parody or critique of standard joke mechanics; practitioners deploy anti-jokes to comment on or mock conventional joke forms. Use this deliberately to subvert expectations or to satirize comedic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately bad performance / persona / performance-art deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor jokes are also often associated with deliberately bad stand-up comedians. Andy Kaufman had his own unique brand of anti-humor, quasi-surrealist acts coupled with performance art; one manifestation was his act as the fictional persona of Tony Clifton, an untalented lounge lizard entertainer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an untalented or awkward persona, or incorporate performance-art elements (fictional characters, deliberately poor delivery) to embody anti-humor. Be mindful this risks alienating audiences; the effect often depends on context and performer commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related forms and contrasts to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-humor is related to or contrasted with forms such as deadpan humor, dad jokes, meta-jokes, nonsense verse, surreal humour, The Aristocrats, koans, 'No soap radio', non sequitur, and conventional riddles like 'Why did the chicken cross the road?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or analyzing anti-humor, consider how it differs from and overlaps with these related genres—e.g., surreal humour violates causal reasoning, meta-jokes reference joke-ness itself—so choose techniques accordingly to position the piece (parodic, surreal, meta, etc.).
